svg.title: The SSH connection to a host
svg.desc: The ferry client runs, for one host, one ssh master, which holds one TCP connection: the host's only SSH connection, so that everything Ferry runs there reaches the same machine, though the host's name may lead to several. The master is your own ControlMaster if your SSH configuration has one, and Ferry's otherwise, its control path ending in %C. Over it runs the host's one session, which sshd starts through the user's login shell: a script that probes the host, installs this build there if it must, and becomes Ferry's monitor there, which listens on a private Unix socket. Everything else goes over channels that sshd forwards to a socket, with no shell: the client follows the monitor on the first, the link between the client's monitor and this one, with a heartbeat each way every 5 seconds; on each other, the monitor starts a ferry server, which has the channel as its standard input and output, its control connection, which it shakes hands over and ends when it closes, and its standard error as its lifeline, which breaks once the monitor is gone. Over it also run the transfer's streams, as many as its round trip needs, one for each 15 ms of it, up to eight, each a channel that sshd forwards to the server's own socket. Where sshd forwards to no socket, the channels reach a port on loopback instead, each giving a secret first; where it forwards to nothing, with --remote-join, each runs ferry server --join through the shell, which hands its input and output over through the socket. The client makes the stream as a socket pair: one end is the channel, the other it hands to the other server, or joins to the other host's channel; it touches none of what goes on it. In order: first, the transport opens the SSH connection, holding an ssh -N: a login only, with no task. Second, the host's one session probes, installs, and becomes the monitor. Third, channels to the monitor: one follows it, and each other has it start a server. Fourth, the client makes the stream. Should the stream break, or the SSH connection drop, the transfer fails: nothing makes it again, as with rsync. Whether the host is there is the heartbeat's to say: once nothing came on the link for 30 seconds, the host is lost, and the transfer fails; the stream and the control connections carry no keepalive, and their silence breaks nothing.
svg.text: watches it, says how it ended
the link: follow the monitor, heartbeat
the streams · a channel each, no shell
The transport opens the SSH connection first, holding an ssh -N: a login only, with no task.
Then the host's one session, through the login shell: it probes, installs Ferry if it must, and becomes Ferry's monitor.
Then channels to the monitor's socket, which run no shell: the link follows it; on each other, it starts a server.
Then the client makes the streams, one for each 15 ms of round trip: should one break, or the connection drop, the transfer fails.
The link's heartbeat says whether the host is there: silent for 30 s, it is lost; the stream's silence breaks nothing.
Where sshd forwards to no socket, a channel reaches a port on loopback instead, with a secret; to nothing, --remote-join.
One SSH connection only: a host's name may lead to several machines, and a second could reach another one.
